1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.strategy: Regains the pawn with the queen, which centralises and attacks the knight on e4 at the same time. Black has to defend or move the knight, and the queen on d4 is later exposed to Black's developing moves. The result is an open game in which White keeps a slight edge and both kings need care.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Centre Attack

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.strategy: Attacks the knight from a safe square and prepares to retake on d4 with the knight. It also sets a trap: defending with ...d5 fails to exd6 en passant, which pins the knight to the king along the e-file. Black has to move the knight again but can equalise.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.background: Wilhelm Steinitz introduced the line in his 1889 book, where he recommended 5.Qe2 over the natural-looking 5.Qxd4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.B.strategy: Pins the d-pawn, so that Black cannot support the e4 knight with ...d5, and keeps the option of regaining the d4 pawn with an attack on the knight. The bishop goes to a square where ...c6 challenges it with tempo, and White's development stalls. Offbeat and double-edged.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.B.name: Petrov's Defence: Modern Attack, Tal Gambit

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d4 exd4 4.e5 Ne4 5.Q.strategy: Takes the knight out of the queen's attack to a square where it eyes e4 and d3, and accepts that White retakes the d4 pawn. Black keeps the piece active and the structure sound, but White has more space, and the knight on c5 gets in the way of the f8 bishop.
